planting.note: Direct-sow into hills once soil is reliably warm, since this long-season landrace needs the full heat of a Gulf Coast summer to size up its fruit.

directions: This is an open-pollinated Florida calabaza released from the state's tropical pumpkin breeding program, grown as a sprawling long-vine type that performs reliably through subtropical heat and humidity. Give it generous room to run, since vines can cover 15 to 25 feet, and let fruit mature fully on the vine for the densest, sweetest orange flesh. It stores well after harvest and holds up better to Gulf Coast disease pressure than many northern pumpkin varieties.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant after frost danger passes; its compact habit fits smaller garden beds better than sprawling calabaza landraces.

directions: Bred at the University of Florida as a compact-plant tropical pumpkin hybrid, this cultivar was developed to give home and market gardeners calabaza-type fruit without the space demands of traditional long-vine landraces like Seminole or La Primera. The restrained vine habit makes it a practical option for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast plots while still tolerating the region's heat and humidity well. Harvest when the rind hardens and dulls for the best storage life.
sources: HortScience (American Society for Horticultural Science journal)

planting.note: Give this large-fruited vine ample hill spacing and a long warm season, since fruit can take the full growing season to size up fully.

directions: Selected in Puerto Rico, this open-pollinated calabaza is prized throughout the Caribbean and Gulf South for its flattened, deeply lobed, dark-green fruit that regularly reaches well over 15 pounds. The dense yellow-orange flesh holds up to long cooking and stores for weeks after a hard-rind harvest. Its vigorous long vines reward generous spacing and thrive in the same heat and humidity that limits many temperate squash varieties.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station

subcategory: perennial legume / dry pea (also used as warm-season cover crop)

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil has fully warmed, since this day-neutral selection flowers on its own schedule rather than waiting for shortening fall daylength.

directions: Developed at the University of Georgia's Tifton research station, this short-duration, day-neutral pigeon pea flowers and sets pods well before fall frost, unlike many tropical pigeon peas that need a long season to trigger bloom. It is a nitrogen-fixing shrub-like legume that tolerates Gulf Coast heat and drought once established, yielding edible green or dry peas as well as a vigorous cover crop. Its semi-determinate, more compact growth habit makes it easier to manage in a vegetable bed than taller tropical pigeon pea types.
sources: ECHO Community (Educational Concerns for Hunger Organization)
